## What Is a Reviewer Maker?


A reviewer maker is a tool that condenses study material into a reviewer: a short study document with the key points, definitions and practice questions for one exam. AI reviewer makers read a PDF, slides, notes or a photo and write that reviewer for you in minutes, so your time goes into practice instead of retyping.


The word "reviewer" has a specific meaning in the Philippines. Students and professionals there use it for the condensed notes and practice items they study before an exam. Common examples are the Licensure Examination for Teachers (LET), the Nurse Licensure Examination (NLE), the CPA Licensure Examination (CPALE), the Civil Service Exam and college entrance tests such as the UPCAT. Review centers publish reviewers, classmates share them, and many students write their own by hand.


Outside the Philippines, the same document goes by other names: a revision sheet, a cram sheet, a study guide or an exam prep pack. The idea is the same everywhere. You take a large body of material and reduce it to the parts the exam will test.


Term Where you hear it What it usually contains


Reviewer Philippines, schools and review centers Key points, definitions, mnemonics, practice items with answers


Revision notes UK, Singapore, Malaysia Condensed topic notes, often with past paper questions


Study guide United States, Canada Outline of topics, terms, sample questions


Cram sheet Professional certifications One or two pages of formulas and must-know facts


Mock exam Everywhere A full timed practice test in the format of the real exam


A good reviewer is narrower than a study guide. A study guide maps a whole course. A reviewer targets one exam, and it is only finished when it includes questions. If you want a broader course document, our sibling guide on[AI study guide makers](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-study-guide-makers) covers that job.


### Why "reviewer maker from PDF" is the search people make


Most exam material arrives as a PDF. Board exam handbooks, review center handouts, lecture slides exported from PowerPoint, and scanned textbook chapters all land as PDF files. A "reviewer maker from PDF" is therefore the first tool a student reaches for when the material is long and the exam date is close.

## A Reviewer Is a Metacognition Tool, Not a Summary


A reviewer works because it tells you what you do not know yet. Metacognition is the ability to monitor and control your own thinking, and psychologist John Flavell described it in a classic 1979 paper ( *American Psychologist* , 34, 906-911). A reviewer that only summarizes skips the monitoring. A reviewer that asks questions forces it.


Here is the trap. When you reread a clean summary, the words feel familiar. Familiar feels like known. Psychologists call this the fluency illusion: smooth rereading creates a sense of mastery that does not predict what you can recall a week later. Robert and Elizabeth Bjork describe the fix as "desirable difficulties" (Bjork and Bjork, 2011, in *Psychology and the Real World* ): conditions that slow you down, such as recall, spacing and mixing topics, build stronger long-term memory than easy review.


A second trap is that people rate their own understanding too high. Rozenblit and Keil (2002, *Cognitive Science* , 26, 521-562) named it the illusion of explanatory depth: people feel they understand how something works until they have to explain it step by step. Kruger and Dunning (1999, *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* , 77, 1121-1134) found that the people who score lowest on a test tend to overestimate their scores the most. A reviewer with questions is the cheapest cure for both.


The neuroscientist Stephen Fleming, author of *Know Thyself: The Science of Self-Awareness* (Basic Books, 2021), studies metacognition by asking people how confident they are after each answer. Good metacognition means your confidence tracks your accuracy. A reviewer with questions gives you that signal every day: you guess, you check, and you learn how far to trust your own feeling of "I know this."


This is why the rest of this guide judges reviewer makers on one main question. Does the tool help you test yourself and see your weak topics, or does it only make the PDF shorter? For a deeper look at the concept, read our explainer on[what metacognition is](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-is-metacognition) .

## Summary Reviewer vs. Question Reviewer: Which Works Better?


A question-based reviewer works better for exam performance than a summary-only reviewer. Summaries help you see how a subject fits together, so they are a good first page. But the evidence on study techniques puts practice testing near the top and rereading near the bottom, so the questions must carry most of the weight.


The largest review of study techniques comes from Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham (2013, *Psychological Science in the Public Interest* , 14, 4-58). They rated ten common techniques. Practice testing and distributed practice (spacing) earned the highest utility rating. Highlighting, rereading and summarization earned low ratings. That does not mean summaries are useless. It means a summary alone is a weak plan for an exam.


Reviewer type What it looks like What it trains Where it fails


Summary reviewer Bullet points per chapter, bold terms, short definitions Recognition and overview Feels complete before you can recall anything


Question reviewer Each topic ends with questions and a hidden answer Recall, the skill the exam measures Takes longer to make by hand


Hybrid reviewer 5 to 10 key points, then 5 to 20 questions per topic Overview first, recall second Needs discipline to answer before you peek


Mock exam Mixed topics, timed, scored by subject Recall under exam conditions Too hard as a first step on a new subject


The hybrid is the format to aim for. Read the key points once to build the map. Then close the key points and answer the questions. Then go back only to the points you missed.


### What a strong reviewer page contains


Every topic in a strong reviewer has the same five parts. The order matters, because the questions come after a short overview and before any long explanation.


Part Purpose Example (LET Professional Education)


Key points Build the map in under two minutes 5 to 8 bullets on a learning theory


Commonly confused pairs Stop the classic wrong answer Formative vs. summative assessment


Practice questions Force recall 10 board-style multiple choice items


Answer key with reasons Fix errors and explain why One sentence per answer on why it is right


Weak-spot note Tell future you what to restudy "Missed 3 of 10 on Bloom's levels"


Commonly confused pairs deserve a special mention. Board exam distractors are often built from the concept next door. A reviewer that lists those pairs side by side, with the one detail that separates them, removes a whole family of wrong answers. Taskade's PDF Reviewer Maker app kit writes these pairs, which is one reason we lead with it below.

Reviewer One exam, condensed Condense, then recall This guide


Flashcards One fact or term per card Rapid recall, spaced repetition[AI flashcard makers](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-flashcard-makers)


Quiz A short set of questions Check one topic[AI quiz generators](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-quiz-generators)


Mock exam The full exam format, timed Recall under pressure[AI exam generators](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-exam-generators)


Many students use all five in one review season. They start from a study guide for the course, condense it into a reviewer for the exam, drill facts with flashcards, quiz each topic, and finish with mock exams. The tools in this guide differ mainly in how far along that chain they take you.

## 2. Gemini Notebook (Formerly NotebookLM): Best for Answers Grounded in Your Sources


Gemini Notebook is Google's source-grounded research and study tool, and it is the same product that was called NotebookLM until Google renamed it on July 16, 2026. You add your PDFs and other sources to a notebook, and its answers stick to those sources with citations back to the passages they came from.


For reviewer work, the Studio panel is the part that matters. According to Google's help center, you can generate Flashcards or Quizzes from your sources with default settings, or customize them first with a difficulty level (easy, medium or hard) and a prompt that sets the focus, style and audience. You set the number of items in the study view (fewer, standard or more). An "Explain" button explains a card or an answer. On flashcards, you mark each card "Got it!" or "Missed it!", your progress is saved, and at the end you can retake the same cards, all cards or only the cards you missed. Flashcards download as a CSV file.


Gemini Notebook at a glance Detail


Input PDFs and other sources added to a notebook


Reviewer output Grounded chat answers with citations, plus written reports


Practice Flashcards and quizzes, easy to hard, with Explain


Retake Same cards, all cards, or only missed cards


Price Free with a Google account, with higher limits on Google AI plans


**Who it is for:** students with many source files who need to trust each answer, and anyone who wants to click from a claim straight to the sentence in the PDF. It is excellent for building the key points of a reviewer, because every point can carry its source.


**Honest limits:** Gemini Notebook is a notebook, not an exam system. It does not run a timed mock exam scored by subject, and it does not track your readiness across weeks. Older guides still call it NotebookLM, so you can find both names in tutorials.

## 3. ChatGPT: Best for Flexible Prompts and Study Mode


ChatGPT is the general-purpose option: you upload a PDF, describe the reviewer you want, and shape the format with your own prompt. Its study mode offers step-by-step guidance instead of quick answers, with guided questions, knowledge checks, quizzes and open-ended questions that show what is sticking.


The strength of ChatGPT is control. You can ask for exactly the reviewer format your review center uses, request commonly confused pairs, set the question style to board-exam multiple choice, and ask for one-sentence explanations under each answer. You can also ask it to quote the line from the PDF that supports each key point, and to say "uncertain" when the PDF does not cover a question. That one instruction cuts a lot of invented detail.

Reviewer output Whatever format you prompt for


Practice Study mode knowledge checks and quizzes

**Who it is for:** students who like to write prompts and want a reviewer in a custom format, and learners who want a patient tutor that asks them questions instead of giving answers.


**Honest limits:** the output lives in a chat, so you copy it elsewhere to keep a reviewer you can study from next week. The Free plan has limited messages with uploads. For a reviewer workflow, Quizlet has two useful paths. The Study Guides tool takes uploaded notes (.docx, .pdf or .pptx files) or up to 100,000 pasted characters, and transforms them into a study guide with flashcards and quizzes. Practice Tests then test you on that material. Learn and Test, Quizlet's classic modes, drill the flashcards themselves.

Knowt's Learn mode mixes multiple choice, true or false, fill-in-the-blank and flashcard questions. A spaced repetition mode is listed among its study options. ## 6. Gizmo: Best for Quiz-Style Drilling on a Phone


Gizmo pitches "AI quizzes that make studying easy" and turns PDFs, notes, slides and YouTube videos into flashcards and quizzes. Its tool list includes PDF to Flashcards, a PDF Summarizer, Notes to Flashcards and PowerPoint to Flashcards. It is built around short, frequent quizzing sessions with a game feel.


For a reviewer workflow, Gizmo is a drill engine rather than a reviewer writer. You generate cards and quiz questions from your PDF, then work through them in short bursts during the day. That habit of many small recall sessions is exactly what spacing and testing research rewards, so a phone-first quiz app can do a lot of good in the weeks before an exam.

## Step-by-Step: PDF to Reviewer to Mock Exam


This workflow takes one PDF to a finished reviewer and a timed mock exam in six steps. It works with any tool on this list, and we show where Taskade handles each step. Plan about one evening for the first subject and less for each subject after it.


### Step 1: Prepare the source


Split a long PDF into topics before you send it to any AI tool. A 300-page handout sent in one piece gives a vague reviewer. One chapter at a time gives a sharp one. If your source is a lecture, turn it into notes first with the[YouTube video to notes converter](https://www.taskade.com/convert/youtube/youtube-video-to-notes) . If it is handwritten, type it up with the[handwritten notes digitizer](https://www.taskade.com/convert/image-to-notes/handwritten-notes-digitizer) . Use only material that you are allowed to use, such as your own notes, your school handouts and public exam coverage documents.


### Step 2: Generate the reviewer with a clear prompt


Ask for the hybrid format, not a summary. In Taskade, the[PDF to Reviewer Maker](https://www.taskade.com/convert/pdf/pdf-to-reviewer) already writes key points and practice questions per section. In a chat tool, paste a prompt like this one:


```text
You are a board exam reviewer writer. From the attached chapter only:
1. Write 5 to 8 key points, one line each.
2. List 3 commonly confused pairs and the one detail that separates each pair.
3. Write 10 multiple choice questions in board exam style, 4 options each.
4. Give the answer key with one sentence on why each answer is right.
5. For every key point, quote the sentence from the chapter that supports it.
If the chapter does not cover something, write "not in source". Do not add outside facts.


```


### Step 3: Check the reviewer against the source


Read each key point next to the quoted sentence. Fix or delete anything that does not match. This step takes 10 minutes per chapter, and it is the step most students skip. It matters because you will memorize whatever the reviewer says.


### Step 4: Answer from memory, then mark misses


Hide the key points and answer the questions. Write your answer before you look at the key. Mark each miss, and also mark each lucky guess, because a correct guess is still a gap.


### Step 5: Build the mock exam


Once you have reviewers for several topics, mix their questions into one test. Match the real exam: the same question style, a similar number of items per subject, and the same time per item. In Taskade, the[PDF Reviewer Maker app kit](https://www.taskade.com/apps/all/pdf-reviewer-maker-reviewers-and-mock-exams-cnxwe08j5irgk0kt) runs timed mock exams for you. You can also generate a scored test with an answer key using the[AI exam generator](https://www.taskade.com/convert/education/education-to-exam) .


### Step 6: Feed the misses back


Score the mock exam by subject. Every subject under your target goes back into the reviewer as a weak topic. Ask the AI for new questions on those topics only, because new questions test understanding, while the same questions again can test memory of the question itself. Then repeat the cycle on a spaced schedule, which the next section explains.

## Spaced Review Before a Board Exam


Spaced review means you return to each topic several times with growing gaps, instead of studying it once in one long session. It is one of the two highest-rated study techniques in Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), and the reviewer is the natural unit to space, because each topic has its own questions.


Two studies by Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues are the main evidence. A 2006 meta-analysis ( *Psychological Bulletin* , 132, 354-380) pooled hundreds of experiments and found that spaced study beats massed study for later recall. A 2008 study ( *Psychological Science* , 19, 1095-1102) tested many combinations of study gap and test delay and found that the best gap grows as the time to the test grows. For a board exam months away, a review gap of a day is too short to be the whole plan.


The chart below shows one example schedule for a single topic. It is a plan, not data from a study.


### A four-phase plan for the months before a board exam


Phase When What you do with the reviewer


Build Early weeks Make one reviewer per topic and answer its questions once


Space Middle weeks Review each topic on day 1, 3, 7 and 14 after you build it


Mix Last 4 to 6 weeks Take mixed-topic quizzes across subjects every few days


Simulate Final weeks Take full timed mock exams and restudy weak subjects only


Mixing topics, called interleaving, is part of the plan for a reason. Kornell and Bjork (2008, *Psychological Science* , 19, 585-592) found that people who studied examples from different categories mixed together learned to tell the categories apart better than people who studied one category at a time, even though most of them believed the blocked method had worked better. A board exam mixes topics, so your late-stage practice must mix them too.


Each topic moves through clear states as you review it. The diagram shows the forward path. When a topic falls below your target in a mock exam, it goes back to the weak list and the cycle restarts for that topic.

## The Learning Science Behind a Good Reviewer


A good reviewer stacks several well-tested effects from memory research: retrieval practice, spacing, generation, self-explanation and interleaving. Each one has a primary study behind it, and each one maps to one feature you can look for in a reviewer maker.


Effect Primary study What it shows Reviewer feature that uses it


Testing effect Roediger and Karpicke, 2006, *Psychological Science* 17, 249-255 Recalling material beats restudying it on delayed tests Practice questions after every topic


Retrieval vs. concept mapping Karpicke and Blunt, 2011, *Science* 331, 772-775 Retrieval practice produced more learning than elaborative study with concept maps Questions over diagrams as the main activity


Spacing effect Cepeda et al., 2006, *Psychological Bulletin* 132, 354-380 Spaced study beats massed study for later recall Scheduled review sessions


Generation effect Slamecka and Graf, 1978, *JEP: Human Learning and Memory* 4, 592-604 Information you produce yourself is remembered better than information you read Answer before you see the key


Self-explanation Chi et al., 1989, *Cognitive Science* 13, 145-182 Learners who explain examples to themselves learn more "Explain why this answer is right" prompts


Interleaving Kornell and Bjork, 2008, *Psychological Science* 19, 585-592 Mixed practice improves telling categories apart Mixed-topic mock exams


The testing effect is the anchor. In Roediger and Karpicke (2006), students who restudied a passage felt more confident in the short term, but students who practiced recall remembered more on a test a week later. A later meta-analysis by Christopher Rowland (2014, *Psychological Bulletin* , 140, 1432-1463) pooled many testing-effect experiments and confirmed that retrieval practice beats restudy on average. That is the scientific case for a question-based reviewer.


The generation effect explains why you must answer before you peek. When you produce an answer, even a wrong one, you do more work than when you read the right one, and that work strengthens memory. Self-explanation explains why an answer key needs reasons. A key that says only "C" teaches you a letter. A key that says why C is right and why B is the classic trap teaches you the concept.


There is a lesson here for AI, too. Mathematician Po-Shen Loh argues that in the AI era the valuable skill is to grade the homework: to check work that a machine produced. A 2025 study by Lee and colleagues at Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University (CHI 2025) surveyed knowledge workers and found that generative AI shifts effort toward verifying and integrating AI output. For a student, that means the AI writes the first draft of the reviewer, and you are the grader. For a hands-on method that uses these effects, read our guide to the[Feynman technique](https://www.taskade.com/blog/feynman-technique) .

## How to Check an AI Reviewer Before You Memorize It


Check every AI reviewer against its source before you study it, because an error you memorize is worse than a topic you never studied. AI tools can misread a table, merge two similar rules, drop a "not" from a sentence, or add a fact from outside your PDF. The check takes minutes and protects weeks of study.


Warning sign What it means What to do


A key point has no source line The AI can have added it from outside your PDF Delete it or find the line yourself


A number differs from the PDF A table or scan was misread Copy the number from the PDF


Two rules look the same The AI merged similar concepts Add them to your confused pairs list


All answers are option C The question set is poorly balanced Ask for a new set with mixed answer positions


A question has two right answers The question is ambiguous Rewrite it or drop it


Tools that cite sources make this step faster. Gemini Notebook links answers to source passages, and StudyPDF says that each claim links to its source page. In Taskade, the AI study agent answers questions about the PDF you added, so you can ask "which section says this?" for any point you doubt.

What is a reviewer maker?

In the Philippines, a reviewer is a condensed study guide for an exam such as the LET, the NLE, the CPALE, the Civil Service Exam or the UPCAT. AI reviewer makers write the key points and practice questions for you, so you can spend your time testing yourself.


Can AI make a reviewer from a PDF?

Taskade, Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), ChatGPT, Quizlet, Knowt, Penseum, Quizbot.ai, Formswrite and StudyPDF all do some version of this. Is a summary reviewer or a question reviewer better?


A question reviewer is better for exam scores. A summary reviewer helps you see the structure of a subject, but rereading a summary feels like learning without proving that you can recall anything. Research on the testing effect, such as Roediger and Karpicke (2006), shows that recalling material beats restudying it on delayed tests. The best reviewer pairs short key points with questions you answer from memory.


How do I turn a reviewer into a mock exam?


Collect the practice questions from every topic of your reviewer, mix the topics together, set a time limit that matches the real exam, and answer without your notes. Score yourself by subject, then send every missed question back into the reviewer as a weak topic. Taskade's PDF Reviewer Maker app kit runs timed mock exams and shows each student's average by subject against a 75 percent target.


When should I start spaced review before a board exam?


Start as early as you can. Spacing research, such as Cepeda and colleagues (2008), found that the best gap between reviews grows with the time you need to remember the material. A practical plan reviews each topic one day, three days, one week and two weeks after you first study it, then switches to full timed mock exams in the final weeks.


Can I make a reviewer from photos of handwritten notes?


Yes, with tools that read images. Penseum, Formswrite, StudyPDF and StudyFetch say that they accept photos or scans of notes. In Taskade, you can digitize handwritten pages with the handwritten notes digitizer and then build the reviewer from the typed text. Check every formula and number after a photo upload, because handwriting is the most common source of reading errors.


Can I trust an AI reviewer for the LET or another board exam?


Use an AI reviewer as a draft, not as the final authority. Check each key point against your source PDF and against the official exam coverage from the board or the review center. Prefer tools that cite the source page, and ask the AI to say when it is unsure. A wrong fact that you memorize costs more than a fact that you never studied.
